content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposes an empirical comparison of some classical clustering algorithms for anomaly detection on a selection of UCI datasets.

I appreciate the effort made by the authors, as skeptical empirical comparisons help us calibrate our compasses as a field. However, the paper in its current state is not ready for publication in a machine learning (ML) venue. A number of recommendations on how to improve it follows. 
First, anomaly detection has grown into a consolidated field, and many recent surveys and systematic comparisons exist, e.g. [1] (which the authors cite) and [2,3]. I suggest authors to build on these efforts, selecting a larger number of methods and dataset benchmarks and, more crucially, arguing why it is important to compare these models. 
Second, presentation can be improved by assuming classical methods are known (e.g., pseudocode of classical clustering algorithms such as K-Means and DBScan can be put in the appendix) and by precisely state the research questions of interest (and designing the experiments to falsify them).

Four knowledgeable reviewers agreed on these points and there was no rebuttal.
The paper is therefore rejected.

[1] Chandola, Varun, Arindam Banerjee, and Vipin Kumar. "Anomaly detection: A survey." ACM computing surveys (CSUR) 41.3 (2009): 1-58.
[2] Chalapathy, Raghavendra, and Sanjay Chawla. "Deep learning for anomaly detection: A survey." arXiv preprint arXiv:1901.03407 (2019).
[3] Goldstein, Markus, and Seiichi Uchida. "A comparative evaluation of unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms for multivariate data." PloS one 11.4 (2016): e0152173.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an empirical comparison of three different clustering/anomaly detection algorithms on six different benchmark data sets. The algorithm performance, in terms of their ability to identify anomalies, is compared and conclusions are presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Such studies are useful for researchers and practitioners.

Weaknesses:
1. The paper is not aligned with the conference. This might make more sense in a data mining conference.
2. The paper does not make many contributions apart from a modest comparative evaluation of methods.
3. The choice of data sets is very dated, I would expect that the authors would pick newer, more challenging data sets.
4. A limited set of anomaly detection algorithms are chosen, and it is not clear why only these are considered.
5. The authors are making conclusions about the methods based on their performance on 6 benchmark data sets. I would like to see some more general analysis because that will be useful for the audience. What kinds of datasets does one method work better for? And why?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and is easy to understand. The experiments seem to the reproducible. The paper does not make any novel contributions for the ICLR community.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is not aligned with the ICLR themes. It is a straightforward comparison of three different clustering based anomaly detection algorithms on 6 benchmark data sets.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents comparison of anomaly detection performance for a few density-based and representative based clustering algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. For such as broad category of algorithms as density based and representative based clustering algorithms, too few algorithms have been compared. Missing ones include Gaussian Mixture Models, Local Outlier Factor, etc. A more exhaustive literature survey should identify more such algorithms.


2. The number and diversity of datasets used in the paper is too little for an empirical study. Most datasets are very small as well.


3. Section 3.4: "In the case of DBSCAN or DBSCAN++ tests more than half of the detected noise points are false positive values indicating that Pima data set does not consist of a density-based cluster structure." -- The directionality of this analysis is wrong. We need to first ascertain the structure of the dataset by some other means and then explain the behavior of the algorithm. In this section, the structure of the dataset is being conjectured from the algorithm behavior.


4. Overall, Section 3.4 presents no new insights. It just confirms that if the data is well-clustered, the class of algorithms under study will work well -- which is already well-known.


5. Section 4: "...we could not run this modified algorithm on all the data sets because of time limitations..." -- Clearly, this work is not complete at this stage.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors present an empirical evaluation of unsupervised anomaly detection using three algorithms (two density-based and one representative based) on six publicly available imbalanced data sets (where the minority class is assumed to be anomalous). Their results show that k-means-- performs better than DBSCAN and DBSCAN++
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The three methods are evaluated on real data sets using multiple metrics



Weaknesses:
- **Methods**: Prior work on anomaly detection is quite rich. The authors do not provide a justification of why only these three methods we selected for evaluation. There are several other well know anomaly detection methods. For example, GMM is not selected although it is better than k-means based algorithms at detecting clusters at multiple scales, and is widely used for anomaly detection. The paper would be stronger if more anomaly detection methods were used. The authors mention that they couldn't find implementation of one of the of the methods they use in sklearn, but sklearn does have a number of other anomaly detection methods (local outlier factor, isolation forest, one-class SVM) that the authors did not compare their methods with. 

- **Data sets**: While the data sets are real-life, I am not sure how representative they are of data sets with anomalies. In two of the data sets, the percentage of anomalies is 35%, which seems too high; these are more data sets with two classes. Real anomalies are typically
very rare (< 1%). Further, in real-life data sets are more complex than two uniform classes as seems to be the case in the data sets used. Typically normal behavior is not just one class, and anomalies are not one class either. Both of these have high variance and usually composed of multiple classes. In this sense, the data sets considered here seem simplistic. 

- **Novelty**:  There is not much novelty in the work as discuss below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly and well written although there are some typos. 

The quality of evaluation is poor since very few methods are compared. The data sets are not representative of real life anomaly detection problems.

There isn't much novelty in the work. The methods are prior work, and no improvements have been make on the methods.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, in my view, this paper is not suitable for publication in ICLR, since it lacks novelty. The evaluation considers only a small subset of anomaly detection algorithms on a small number of data sets, which may not be representative of anomaly detection data sets It is unclear how generalizable these results.

content.title: An Empirical Study on Anomaly detection Using Density Based and Representative Based Clustering algorithms
content.TL;DR: In this paper, we focus on existing anomaly detection approaches, by empirically studying the performance of unsupervised anomaly detection techniques.
content.abstract: In data mining, and statistics, anomaly detection is the process of finding data patterns (outcomes, values, or observations) that deviate from the rest of the d other observations or outcomes.  Anomaly detection is heavily used in solving real-world problems in many application domains like medicine, finance, cybersecurity, banking, networking, transportation, and military surveillance for enemy activities, but not limited to only those fields. In this paper, we present an empirical study of unsupervised anomaly detection techniques such as DBSCAN, DBSCAN++ (with uniform initialization, k-center initialization, uniform with approximate neighbor initialization, and k-center with approximate neighbor initialization), and k-means --(minus minus) algorithms on six benchmark imbalanced datasets.  Findings from our in-depth empirical study show that k-means -- is a robust than DBSCAN, and DBSCAN++, in terms of the different evaluation measures (F1 score, False alarm rate, adjusted rand index, and Jaccard coefficient), and running time. We also observe that DBSCAN performs very well on datasets with fewer number of data points.
